claims.text: Adding TiC nanoparticles to a refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its radiation tolerance.
Adding TiC nanoparticles can preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity while improving radiation tolerance.
Adding TiC nanoparticles is an engineering-practical intervention.
The intervention produces a distribution and dispersion of TiC nanoparticles within the alloy matrix.
TiC nanoparticles act as sinks for radiation-induced defects.
Defect capture by TiC nanoparticles reduces the accumulation of irradiation damage.
Reduced defect accumulation increases resistance to radiation hardening.
Reduced defect accumulation increases resistance to irradiation-induced embrittlement.
The modified alloy will exhibit a 20% increase in the critical irradiation dose for the onset of significant hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will retain 10% more ductility after irradiation than the unmodified alloy.
The proposed benefit should hold at operating temperatures from 500°C to 1000°C.
The proposed benefit should hold at irradiation doses up to 100 dpa.
The proposed benefit should hold when applied stress does not exceed the alloy's yield strength.
The proposed effect should hold for TiC nanoparticle concentrations between 0.5 and 2.0 vol%.
The proposed effect may diminish or disappear outside the range of 0.5 to 2.0 vol% TiC nanoparticles.
